source: Klahr and Dunbar (1988) Dual space search during scientific reasoning (Study 1, overall)
finding: Adults learned BigTrak (a programmable toy vehicle), then had to find out what its unexplained REPEAT key does. Almost all solved it, but only after wrong first guesses. No subject began with the correct rule.
numbers: Study 1: 20 CMU undergraduates, 45 min limit. 19 of 20 found the rule. Mean time to solution 19.8 min (SD 9.6). Mean 18.2 programs (SD 11.5). 364 programs in all: 304 experiments, 51 control trials, 7 calibration trials. 17 of 20 started with the 'N means number of repeats' frame. About 28% of experiments had no stated hypothesis.
limits: Small student sample, one toy device, one rule. Programming knowledge was not controlled in advance (see d02).
agent_relevance: This is the human bar for a hidden-rule task: about 95% solve it in under an hour, with about 18 tries. An LLM trace can be scored on the same two things: tries to solution and share of experiments run with no stated hypothesis.

source: Klahr and Dunbar (1988) Study 1: Theorists versus Experimenters
finding: Subjects split by how they escaped the wrong frame. Seven 'Theorists' got the right frame by searching memory (hypothesis space). Thirteen 'Experimenters' got it only after an experiment in a key region of the experiment space showed the last N steps repeated. The hypothesis space stalled for 13 of 20 people; the experiment space rescued them.
numbers: Experimenters (N=13) vs Theorists (N=7): time 24.46 vs 11.40 min (t(18)=3.97, p<.0009); experiments 18.33 vs 9.29 (t(18)=3.09, p<.006); experiments with no stated hypothesis 6.08 vs 0.76 (t(18)=3.70, p<.002); different hypotheses 4.92 vs 3.06 (p<.08, n.s.). All 7 Theorists but only 1 Experimenter had programming experience. Across 220 outcomes: when an experiment confirmed the current hypothesis, subjects dropped it in 25% of cases (21/84); when it disconfirmed, they kept it in over half (76/136).
quote: Subjects who could not think of the correct rule in the hypothesis generation phase discovered the correct rule only by generalizing from the results of experiments
limits: The groups were formed after the fact from behaviour, and prior programming knowledge is confounded with strategy. Not a randomised comparison.
agent_relevance: Direct test for the dual-space reading on LLM traces: count how often a model leaves a wrong frame because of an experiment result versus a recalled idea. Also the 'keeps a disconfirmed hypothesis' rate (about 4 of 11 outcomes per person) is a number to compare with a scaffold that forces a switch after a miss.

source: Klahr and Dunbar (1988) Study 2: state all hypotheses before any experiment
finding: Ten adults first listed every hypothesis they could think of, then experimented. Half already named the right rule in the listing phase. The other half still found it fast once they could run experiments. Having a prior list shortened the search for everyone.
numbers: N=10. Mean 4.2 hypotheses listed. 5 of 10 stated the correct rule in phase 1 (4 Theorists, 1 Experimenter; the 4 Theorists all had programming experience, only 1 of 6 Experimenters did). Phase 2: all 10 solved it; mean 6.2 min, 5.7 experiments, 2.4 hypotheses. Theorists 3.3 min and 3.0 experiments (N=4); Experimenters 8.2 min and 7.5 experiments (N=6). In study 1 under 10% of experiments used the right frame; in study 2 half the subjects proposed it.
limits: Tiny N. The listing phase may itself change behaviour (it is not a pure measurement of what people would have thought of).
agent_relevance: Supports a 'list rival hypotheses first, then run discriminating tests' step. Phase 1 gives a cheap test: does the model's first list contain the true frame at all? If not, only experiments can rescue it.

source: Huang et al. (2026) Can LLMs discover scientific laws in real and parallel worlds? (SciLaws-Bench, main table)
finding: New benchmark: 118 problems from 381 papers, 14 models in one shared ReAct harness (30 turns, Python sandbox, medium reasoning effort). Newest models lead, but fit and structure recovery stay low. GPT-6 was the best on every column.
numbers: SciLaws-Real normalised fit SN (50 = published baseline): GPT-6 51.33, GPT-5.5 50.11, Claude Opus 5.5 48.87, Kimi K3 47.36, Gemini 3.5 Flash 46.08, GLM-5.2 45.84, Opus 4.8 44.94, DeepSeek-V4 Pro 43.96, GPT-4o-mini 20.59. Validity SV: GPT-6 82.91 vs GPT-4o-mini 56.02. SciLaws-Parallel structure score SS: GPT-6 72.46, Opus 5.5 58.69, GPT-5.5 58.26, GPT-4o-mini 33.47. Runs returning a formula 90 to 99% for thinking models.
limits: Authors' own benchmark. Judges are LLMs (GPT-5.4-mini; kappa 0.82 validity, 0.84 structure vs five experts). No arm with a different scaffold, so it cannot say what a scaffold adds. Models were run at medium effort with 65,536 output tokens.
agent_relevance: Gives current-model numbers (2026) that older papers lack. The 14 points GPT-6 gained over GPT-5.5 on SS show backbone changes can swamp a scaffold effect, so scaffold tests must hold the backbone fixed.

source: Huang et al. (2026) SciLaws-Bench: memorisation audit by recall tier
finding: A cold-recall audit (can the model write the published formula from variable names alone) split tasks into Canon (11), Mid (61) and Moat (46). Recall helps recover the published form but does NOT help recover a new structural variant. Full-law recovery was flat across tiers.
numbers: Universal recall limited to 9.3% of tasks; 39.0% were recalled by no model. Best recall: Claude Opus 5.5 reproduced only 44.1% of reference formulas. SciLaws-Parallel published-form recovery: 92% (Canon) to 61% (Moat). Full-law recovery 12 to 13% across all tiers. GPT-6 full-law 42% overall and 39% on Moat; GPT-4o-mini 0%. Real: share of solutions beating the published baseline rose from 12% (Canon) to 36% (Moat) on average. Beer-Lambert: all 14 models got the published form, none the full hidden law.
limits: Recall is judged by an LLM (GPT-4.1, kappa 0.77), 3 of 5 samples must match. Tier labels depend on this model set.
agent_relevance: A usable recall control: classify each task by whether the model can cold-recall the answer. It predicts published-form recovery but not new-structure recovery, so score new-structure recovery separately. Answers part of gap 10: a recall-tier split is cheaper than building altered laws, but it measures something different.

source: Huang et al. (2026) SciLaws-Bench: finding versus choosing the law (search and selection)
finding: Agents often evaluate a better law during the run than the one they submit. Choosing among finished candidates with the same model, with no score feedback, recovers little of the headroom.
numbers: Best candidate in a run versus submitted law, mean gap in SN: 0.14 for GPT-5.4-mini, 0.03 to 0.04 for GPT-6 and Opus 5.5. Best-of-N (GPT-5.4-mini, all 118 tasks, pools of 20): from N=5 to N=20 the oracle gains 4.5 points (SN) and 5.3 points (SV); self-selection gains under 2 points. 60% of selected winners were Pareto-dominated by another candidate in the group of five.
limits: Gap measured offline with held-out data, which the agent does not see. The selector was never given a held-out check, so the paper does not test one. One weak model for best-of-N.
agent_relevance: Strong hint for the held-out-check idea (gap 3): the failure is selection, not generation, and it is bigger for weaker models. A code step that scores every candidate on a held-out split before submit is the direct test. Not yet tested at equal tokens.

source: Huang et al. (2026) SciLaws-Bench: fit versus scientific validity
finding: Better numeric fit did not reliably mean a more valid law. Within one task, fit and validity agreed on which of two models was better in only 53.6% of 9,279 unequal-fit pairs.
numbers: Concordance 53.6% (chance 50%), rising to 66.4% only when the fit margin is at least 0.4. Across models mean fit and structure scores correlate r=0.83, but within GPT-6 across tasks only r=0.06. Keeling task: GPT-5.5 beats the reference on Real but recovers only the trend on Parallel. Sellmeier: the reverse.
limits: Validity rubric is applied by an LLM judge. Strict scoring convention.
agent_relevance: Confirms fit alone is a poor accept rule. A claim-versus-output code check (does the stated law reproduce the executed numbers, and obey bounds and monotonicity rules) is a plausible extra filter; this paper does not test that filter.

source: Yao et al. (2026) Library reachability in LSR-Synth (paired BANK, LLM, UNION arms)
finding: A fixed list of generic terms (powers, exp, log, trig, simple products) that never reads variable names solved most LLM-SRBench synthetic tasks. Adding LLM-proposed terms added almost nothing unless the fixed list was cut down to polynomials.
numbers: 129 LSR-Synth tasks, 4 paired seeds, same 800-point fitter and search budget in every arm. BANK-LaSR: Acc0.01 77.71, Acc0.001 62.60, strict ID+OOD 39.53, symbolic accuracy 19.77. LLM alone (named variables): 49.81 / 30.81 / 13.76 / 8.14. UNION (bank plus LLM): 77.33 to 77.71 (no gain). Poly-only bank 27.52; UNION-Poly-L1 58.14 (+30.6). Best earlier reports on the same 129 tasks: SR-Scientist 63.57, LLM-SR 41.08, PySR 29.46, LaSR 16.02.
limits: Only the LLM-SRBench synthetic split, one LLM-term generator (it proposes 14 terms; code then forms products), one fitter. The tasks use familiar building blocks. The authors say this does not prove LLM priors are useless.
agent_relevance: Correct for the headline 'LLM beats search': a free semantic-blind library matches it. Any scaffold claim needs a no-LLM bank arm at the same fitting budget. Also supports 'code does the fitting, model adds structure only where the library has a hole'.

source: Yao et al. (2026) Library reachability: semantic blinding and unique successes
finding: Hiding variable names and the domain text lowered LLM term quality, so names and context do carry signal. But the bank still covered more tasks than the LLM did.
numbers: L1 (names + domain) vs L2 (anonymous x1, x2): Acc0.01 49.81 vs 41.09; strict ID+OOD 13.76 vs 6.59; symbolic accuracy 8.14 vs 2.71. Of 257 L1 successes 254 also solved by BANK; of 212 L2 successes 210 (LLM unique: 3 and 2). At the stricter symbolic-accuracy bar LLM-only 26 (L1) and 12 (L2) structures vs BANK-only 86 and 100. Out-of-distribution scoring lowers all rates but not the order.
limits: Symbolic accuracy needs 10 of 10 LLM-judge votes (GPT-OSS-120B); the authors note it stays judge-dependent. A 15-task pilot with an equal-size irrelevant-term control has a confidence interval that includes zero.
agent_relevance: Helps gap 10: variable renaming (L1 vs L2) gave a clean, graded recall control (about 8 to 9 points of Acc0.01) and the OOD split kept the ranking. Use renaming plus a no-LLM bank as paired controls.

source: Xie et al. (2026) Language models guide symbolic equation discovery by controlling search (LLM-PySR)
finding: Same GPT-5.1 backbone, same compute budget, five role splits. Letting the model set up the search (variables, operators, depth) while PySR enumerates and numeric gates keep or drop candidates did best and cost the least tokens. Letting the model write equations or judge candidates did worse.
numbers: 74 AI-Feynman equations, mean ACC0.1 / NMSE / tokens: search controller 0.958 / 0.034 / 91k; candidate decider 0.952 / 0.030 / 103k; no-LLM PySR 0.922 / 0.104 / none; equation author 0.892 / 0.387 / 450k; LLM-SR 0.892 / 0.051 / 2.21M; DrSR 0.665 / 0.169 / 2.84M. Controller used 4.1% and 3.2% of the tokens of LLM-SR and DrSR. Controller minus plain PySR: +3.6 points ACC0.1.
limits: One backbone (GPT-5.1). AI Feynman is public, so recall may help every arm. The gain over plain PySR is small and standard deviations are large (0.165). Authors' own method. One real case (battery, 40 test cells).
agent_relevance: The closest thing in the set to an equal-compute role test. Supports keeping retention decisions in code (numeric gates). It does not show a scaffold beats a plain reasoning model; the plain-LLM arm is LLM-SR, not a reasoning model with code.

source: Xie et al. (2026) LLM-PySR: seven stress tests and failure modes
finding: Model-written equations collapsed on atypical formulas; model-judged retention failed on a standard one. Search control was the only role that did well on both.
numbers: Seven complex tasks. Author and full-LLM roles near perfect on familiar forms (CRK0, oscillator1) but 'catastrophic collapse' on bactgrow and stressstrain. Candidate decider did badly on oscillator2 although the correct candidate was in the pool. Controller had lower between-run variance than the decider.
limits: Qualitative heat map; seven cases only; no repeat count stated in the main text.
agent_relevance: Gives a boundary: recall-driven generation fails off the familiar; LLM selection fails on near-ties. Both are cases a code-side check can cover.

source: Yang et al. (2026) KeplerAgent: symmetry and structure tools before symbolic regression (differential equations)
finding: An agent that first runs structure tools (symmetry finder, plot reader) and then configures PySR or PySINDy beat plain PySR and LLM-SR on coupled equations, especially with noise, at far lower cost.
numbers: DiffEq set: 10 systems, 20 equations. Symbolic accuracy clean/noisy: KeplerAgent 75/45, LLM-SR 40/15, PySR 30/10. Tokens about 23k to 30k for KeplerAgent versus 182k to 184k for LLM-SR; runtime about 120 to 147 s vs about 3,650 to 4,050 s for PySR. All LLM parts use GPT-4o-mini.
limits: Weak backbone. Authors' own DiffEq benchmark with 20 equations. Symbolic accuracy judged by GPT-4o-mini. NMSE means are dominated by outliers. Tools used: symmetry detection, visual subagent, not units or separability. Row-to-method mapping read from a garbled table; the text confirms 45% noisy is 3 times the best baseline.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 5: a code-run structure probe lifted a weak LLM agent a lot, and the lift held under noise. Units and separability probes were not tested here.

source: Yang et al. (2026) KeplerAgent on LSR-Transform (changed-law style task)
finding: On the 111 LSR-Transform equations the structure-guided agent did not beat plain PySR in one run; it needed the best of 3 runs.
numbers: Symbolic accuracy: PySR 37.84, LLM-SR 31.53 (from the LLM-SRBench paper), KeplerAgent one run 35.14, best of 3 runs 42.34. Runtime 2440 s PySR vs 238 s (one run). Tokens used by KeplerAgent roughly 42k to 209k depending on setting (table partly garbled).
limits: Best-of-3 chosen on test NMSE is a selection step the baselines lack. GPT-4o-mini backbone. LSR-Transform is a transformed-Feynman set where recall can still help (SR-Scientist footnote says nearly 50% reach low error after one try).
agent_relevance: Boundary for gap 5: on transformed, non-ODE targets a structure probe gave little (-2.7 points in one run vs PySR). The big lifts came on ODE systems where symmetry exists.

source: Zheng et al. (2026) NewtonBench: code budget experiment and LLM-SR comparison (appendix E)
finding: Gap-3 evidence re-read. The harm from code access shows up when the code budget goes from zero to one call for stronger models; exploration language in the trace drops for Gemini-2.5-flash but stays flat for Qwen-3-235b. The authors infer early settling from this.
numbers: Four models tested at several code budgets. Exploration rate computed from signature phrases ('What if', 'Alternatively' vs 'Confirm', 'Verify') in two reasoning models' traces. GPT-5-mini uses code mostly for function fitting, GPT-4.1 more for arithmetic. Separate: LLM-SR (GPT-4.1-mini, 2,500 iterations, about 10,000 API calls, 1,000 times the agent's calls) on the simplest domain (sound speed): symbolic accuracy 55.6 vs PySR 36.1; authors report their code-assisted agent still scored higher.
limits: Cause is inferred from phrase counts in two traces, not tested by an intervention. LLM-SR was run on one domain, with relaxed scoring after post-processing. No minimum-hypotheses rule or held-out check was tried.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 is still open: nobody has run the rule 'list at least k distinct rival laws before first fit' or 'check on held-out points before stopping' against code access at equal tokens. The data show where to look: the first code call.

source: Saveliev et al. (2026) Influence-guided symbolic regression (IGSR) at a fixed 300k-token budget
finding: Per-term feedback (how much each model term helps held-out error) plus pruning in a tree search beat LLM-SR, LaSR and in-context baselines at the same token budget on LLM-SRBench.
numbers: 128 LLM-SRBench discovery problems, 300k tokens per run, GPT-4o-mini, 5 seeds. Average rank (lower is better), ID NMSE: IGSR 1.35, IGSR-Agent 2.41, LLM-SR 3.71, ICL 3.91, ICSR 4.21, LaSR 5.53. Term recall rank: IGSR 1.99, LLM-SR 3.13, LaSR 4.60. Symbolic accuracy ranks are close (1.17 vs 1.29 to 1.35).
limits: Average ranks hide effect size. Weak backbone (GPT-4o-mini). Authors' method. Symbolic-accuracy gap is small. No reasoning-model baseline.
agent_relevance: Evidence that scoring parts of a candidate on held-out data (credit assignment) beats a single score at equal tokens. It does not answer whether a strong reasoning model needs it.

source: Wang et al. (2026) FIRE-Bench: failure stages and cutoff table (re-read for gaps 9 and 10)
finding: Rediscovery of 30+ ML findings. All agents fail in the same places: research planning and conclusion formation, not code. Tasks published after a model's cutoff were not harder.
numbers: Claude Code (Sonnet-4) F1 46.7, Codex (gpt-5 medium) 41.9, OpenHands gpt-5 37.9, o4-mini 31.9. False-positive claims: contradictory plus unrelated 76.4 to 95.0%, alternative-but-plausible only 4.5 to 10.9%. Cutoffs 2024-06-01 (o4-mini), 2024-09-30 (gpt-5). Pre vs post cutoff F1, gpt-5: easy 62.3 vs 61.6 (n=6 vs 1), medium 44.5 vs 23.1 (7 vs 6), hard 22.6 vs 31.0 (5 vs 5). Ten cross-domain tasks: F1 under 25 for all three agents.
limits: Cells have 1 to 8 tasks; wide spread (SD up to 24). Stage shares are shown only in a pie chart, so exact percentages were not read. Judge is an LLM (gpt-5.2). The paper does not test a code check of claim against output.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 only half closed: control design and conclusions are the failure sites, but the 'would a code check help' question is untested. Gap 10: with cells this small the cutoff split cannot rank recall controls.

source: Search log: LLM studies of Klahr-style dual-space coding, STAHL-style historical-order feeding, and conditional-law learning
finding: Negative result, not a source. Searches this session found no LLM study that (a) codes agent traces as hypothesis-space versus experiment-space search, (b) feeds an LLM a historical case series in order and checks for the historical wrong turns, or (c) tests scope-tagged (condition-split) revision against overwrite. The arXiv API returned HTTP 429 after the first batch of queries and WebSearch hit its session budget, so the negative is weak.
numbers: About 10 arXiv API queries before the rate limit (equation discovery, law discovery, scientific law, AI Feynman with LLM, Klahr with language model). Zero hits for the three topics above. SciLaws-Bench (d04) does include multi-group tasks with one shared form and group-specific parameters, which is a limited conditional case.
limits: Absence of evidence under rate limits. A fresh search with working quotas should retry before this is treated as settled.
agent_relevance: Gaps 7 and 8 stay open and look like real research holes, so a test the project builds would be new, not a replication.

source: Qin and Simon (1990) and Klahr and Simon (1999): access attempt
finding: Not read. Crossref gave the DOIs (10.1207/s15516709cog1402_4 and 10.1037/0033-2909.125.5.524). The Wiley and APA PDFs returned 403 or a loading shell, and the guessed author-page PDFs 404ed, so no numbers were taken from them.
numbers: No numbers recorded. The claim K26 (4 of 14 subjects found Kepler's third law) is still from a search summary only.
limits: Paywalled; WebSearch quota gone; OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar rate-limited.
agent_relevance: Do not cite K26 or the Klahr and Simon (1999) review figures as read. Klahr and Dunbar (1988) is now read (d01 to d03) and is the only human bar with checked numbers.
